titulo: Reading the training: curves, collapse, and reward hacking
lead: A reward curve going up does not mean the robot learned to walk. In this lesson you read the log of your own training and of two real 150-iteration trainings, recorded for the course: in one of them the reward goes up because the robot learned to fall sooner. The other shows the fix and the limit of the fix.
objetivo: read the log of a training run and recognize collapse and reward hacking.

aprende.t: Reward, episode length, and speed: the three numbers read together
Reward hacking: it went from −4.31 to −1.12 while the episode dropped from 55 to 15 steps
The fix with is_alive and its limit: 0.16 m/s
The train → read → adjust → train again cycle

hero_alt: A monitor on a dark bench with a blurred line chart going up, and a humanoid robot standing upright, held by a gantry, in the background.

secoes.sub: Click each block. Each alert compares the first and the last quarter of the training.

nos.detalhe: Reward summed per episode, averaged over the episodes of each iteration. On its own it misleads: it goes up when the robot learns, but also when it finds a shortcut.
How many steps the robot stays upright, on average. Shorter episode = falling sooner. If the reward goes up and the episode gets shorter, alert.
The average vx at the end. A reward going up with the robot almost stopped (below 0.1 m/s) also becomes an alert.
The progresso.csv stores each term per iteration. The term that pays the most at the end tells you what the policy actually optimized.

secoes.legenda: Walking on its knees, shaking, and standing still are the classic shortcuts. All of them show up when you read these four numbers together, never the reward alone.

abas.html:
treino: ppo · 20 iterações (médias do primeiro e do último quarto)
recompensa inicial: -3.64 · final: -4.75
episódio médio: 46 → 58 passos (de 1000)
velocidade para a frente no fim: 0.14 m/s · termo que mais pagou no fim: pose (1.00)
alertas: 0
saída: 0

In 20 iterations the reward still oscillates and the term that pays the most is pose: the policy has barely left the default pose. No alerts, but nothing to learn from either. That is why the kit includes two larger training runs. Careful: curvas.py exits 0 even with an alert; read the alertas: line, not the exit code.

secoes.sub: Generated with the same kit/treinar.py, 32 environments, seed 0. cai-cedo uses kit/recompensa.yaml (8 min); com-vivo adds the is_alive term with weight 5 (10 min). Only the progresso.csv is in the repository.

blocos.conteudo: is_alive: {weight: 5.0}                            # 5 × 0,02 s = +0,1 por passo de pé: ficar vivo passa a valer mais que a puniçêo

F=${FTH:-$HOME/fth}; cd $F/locomocao && . $F/.venv/bin/activate
for x in cai-cedo com-vivo; do python3 kit/curvas.py kit/exemplos/$x; echo; done

abas.html:
treino: cai-cedo · 150 iterações (médias do primeiro e do último quarto)
recompensa inicial: -4.31 · final: -1.12
episódio médio: 55 → 15 passos (de 1000)
velocidade para a frente no fim: 0.15 m/s · termo que mais pagou no fim: upright (0.23)
ALERTA: recompensa hackeada: a recompensa subiu porque o episódio encurtou; cada passo de pé custa mais do que paga, e cair cedo virou a melhor estratégia
alertas: 1

treino: com-vivo · 150 iterações (médias do primeiro e do último quarto)
recompensa inicial: 1.36 · final: 2.32
episódio médio: 57 → 63 passos (de 1000)
velocidade para a frente no fim: 0.16 m/s · termo que mais pagou no fim: is_alive (6.27)
alertas: 0

cai-cedo: the reward rose from −4.31 to −1.12 while the episode dropped from 55 to 15 steps. Since every step spent standing had a negative balance (the penalty for abrupt actions outweighed the rewards), falling early became the best strategy.

com-vivo: with is_alive weight 5 (+0.1 per step standing, 5 per second), the episode starts to grow (57 → 63) and no alert fires. But the term that pays the most is is_alive and the speed is 0.16 m/s: the training learned not to fall, not yet to walk.

secoes.sub: Run it, watch the curve reading stop the training, and run it again. This is the loop of this lesson.

msg.rodando: One step at a time: it only trains again after you read and tune.
msg.parou: Stopped. Run it again: the interrupted step starts over, the earlier ones still count.
msg.retoma: Resumed: what was already done is not repeated.
msg.fim: Cycle complete: the tuned training moves on to evaluation.
msg.fimfalha: The curves flagged reward hacking (episode getting shorter while the reward goes up). Tune one term and train again.

secoes.legenda: Illustrative simulation in the browser. The alert in the curve reading is on purpose: it is the cai-cedo case.

exercicios.texto: Run curvas.py on the lesson 5 training and write down the term that paid the most at the end.
Run both examples and write, in one sentence, why the reward in cai-cedo went up.
exercicios.pronto: the cai-cedo output shows ALERTA: recompensa hackeada and alertas: 1; your sentence mentions the episode getting shorter (55 → 15 steps).

exercicios.texto: The com-vivo doesn't fall, but it walks at 0.16 m/s. Propose a tweak to one term (which one, old weight, new weight) and say what signal you would expect to see in the curves if it works.
exercicios.pronto: you wrote one term from kit/recompensa.yaml with both weights and a measurable signal (e.g., final speed above 0.3 m/s without the episode getting shorter).

secoes.sub: The explanation appears after your answer.

perguntas.p: In cai-cedo, the reward went up and the episode dropped from 55 to 15 steps. What did the policy learn?
opcoes: To walk faster, finishing the course ahead of time.
To stand still, without spending energy on the gait.
To fall early, because every step spent standing gave a negative balance.
Nothing: it's noise from a single bad iteration.
perguntas.explica: With a negative balance on every step spent standing, fewer steps = less penalty. curvas.py compares whole quarters of the training run precisely so it does not mistake this for noise.

perguntas.p: The com-vivo triggers no alert. Why is it still not a good training run?
opcoes: Because is_alive is forbidden in humanoid RL repositories.
Because 150 iterations are always enough to walk, and it should already be walking at 0.7 m/s.
Because the reward became positive, which indicates an error in the log.
What pays the most is staying alive and the speed is 0.16 m/s: it doesn't fall, but it doesn't walk.
perguntas.explica: No alert is not the same as correct. A large is_alive removes the shortcut of falling, but it can create the shortcut of standing still; unitree_rl_lab uses only 0.15.

perguntas.p: Which reading detects "reward hacking" most reliably?
opcoes: Reward, episode length, and speed read together.
The average reward of the last training iteration.
The highest value the reward reached in any training iteration.
The total training time compared with what was planned.
perguntas.explica: A single number always has a shortcut that fools it. Three signals and the dominant term together close the most common doors.

perguntas.p: Why does the kit keep two example training runs instead of asking you to run 150 iterations?
opcoes: Because kit/treinar.py does not accept more than 20 iterations.
Because they take 8 to 10 min on CPU, and reading them is what the lesson teaches.
Because the result changes on every run, so you couldn't compare.
Because the examples were trained on the GPU and can't be repeated on CPU.
perguntas.explica: You can repeat them (the commands are in kit/exemplos/LEIA.md). But the skill in this lesson is reading; the training time is optional.

itens.texto: Reward, episode length, speed and dominant term, always together.
In cai-cedo, the reward went up because the robot learned to fall sooner.
Train, read, adjust one term and train again; with no alert it still isn't walking.
